common_name: Papaya Popsicle Red Hot Poker (Compact Peachy-Pink Dwarf Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; part of the compact Popsicle series bred for smaller borders and container growing.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, siting the crown where winter moisture cannot pool around it. Papaya Popsicle carries the same dwarf, compact habit as its sibling Mango Popsicle but opens in a softer peachy-pink to salmon-orange rather than pure mango-orange, fading paler toward the base of each torch-shaped spike as florets age. Its short grassy foliage and reduced overall size fit rock gardens, containers, and the front of a mixed border where full-size kniphofias would overwhelm the scale. Hummingbirds visit the tubular flowers through the summer bloom period; divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring once flowering begins to decline.

common_name: Dwarf Red Hot Poker (Narrow-Leaved Autumn Torch Lily)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or plant divisions/container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; sharp drainage through winter is essential, as with all kniphofias. This dwarf, narrow-leaved species from the high Drakensberg grasslands of South Africa forms tidy, grassy tufts distinctly finer-textured than the large hybrid red hot pokers, sending up slender, deep orange-red torches in late summer into autumn, later than most garden Kniphofia hybrids. Its smaller scale and late bloom period make it a valuable front-of-border or rock-garden choice that extends the red-hot-poker season into fall, when it draws late-migrating hummingbirds. Divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Little Maid Red Hot Poker (Compact Ivory Torch Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this Beth Chatto-raised selection stays compact and clump-forming rather than spreading.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; good winter drainage is essential, since standing moisture around the crown causes rot. Little Maid is a long-popular, RHS Award of Garden Merit dwarf selection bearing slender spikes of pale, soft yellow buds that open to creamy ivory-white, a gentler effect than the hot reds and oranges typical of the genus, blooming from midsummer into early autumn above tidy, fine, grassy foliage. Its compact, well-behaved clumping habit suits smaller borders, gravel gardens, and mixed perennial plantings where taller kniphofia hybrids would be out of scale. Divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Stalked Red Hot Poker (Blue-Leaved Torch Lily)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or plant divisions/container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant kniphofia species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; established clumps tolerate more winter cold and wet than most kniphofias, but drainage still matters most in the first year or two. This South African species forms a striking, architectural rosette of broad, succulent, blue-grey leaves that persist as an evergreen mound even without flowers, eventually developing a short, thick, trunk-like stem with age that gives the species its name. In late summer into autumn, sturdy spikes carry dense, coral-pink to salmon flower heads that age to cream as they open from the top down, held well above the foliage. An RHS Award of Garden Merit species valued as much for its bold, blue-toned foliage texture as for its late-season flowers; leave clumps undivided for years to let the architectural rosette develop fully.

common_name: Zeal Giant Nerine (Large-Flowered Hardy Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun against a warm wall or border for best flowering.

directions: Set bulbs shallowly, with the tip barely covered, in gritty, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, ideally at the base of a warm south-facing wall. Zeal Giant is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection of the hardiest nerine species, chosen for its unusually large individual flowers and full umbels of deep pink, reflexed, wavy-edged blooms on strong bare stems in early to mid autumn, ahead of the strap-shaped leaves. Leave clumps undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as bulbs become congested, and withhold summer water once foliage dies back to respect its dry dormancy period. Where winters are wetter or colder than zone 7 allows, mulch heavily in fall or grow in pots moved under cover for winter.

common_name: Corusca Major Nerine (Iridescent Scarlet-Orange Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer or early fall with the neck at or just at soil surface in very well-drained, gritty, slightly alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Plant bulbs in late summer with the neck at soil surface in very well-drained, gritty, sandy to loamy, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, and keep bulbs nearly dry through their late spring and summer dormancy. Corusca Major is one of the oldest named Nerine sarniensis selections still in cultivation, prized for its vivid scarlet-orange flowers with the same crystalline, light-scattering petal surface that gives the species its glittering, metallic sheen, in unusually large, full umbels on bare stems in autumn before the strap-shaped leaves appear. Because it needs a dry, frost-free summer rest and sharp winter drainage, it performs most reliably in a bulb frame, greenhouse, or pot moved under cover outside of true Mediterranean or Cape-climate gardens. An excellent, long-lasting cut flower with a long history as a florist's favorite since the 17th century.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Plant with the bulb neck just at or above soil level in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and reduce water once foliage yellows for summer dormancy. This slender South African species, long grown as Nerine flexuosa, produces narrow, strap-shaped leaves and loose umbels of pale to soft pink flowers with distinctively wavy, ribbon-like, undulating petal margins, opening in autumn on bare stems ahead of or alongside the foliage. It is nearly as cold-hardy as N. bowdenii and spreads more readily into naturalized colonies, making it a good choice for autumn bulb drifts along a warm, sheltered border edge. Leave clumps undisturbed for best flowering, and mulch over winter in the colder parts of its range.
scientific_name_note: Long cultivated and still often sold as Nerine flexuosa; N. undulata is the currently accepted name.

common_name: Octopus Pineapple Lily (Dwarf Spotted Pineapple Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after the soil has warmed in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; excellent in containers that can be moved under cover for winter.

directions: Plant bulbs about two to three inches deep after danger of frost has passed, in gritty, fertile, well-drained soil, siting in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates. This dwarf South African species, widely sold under the trade name Octopus, forms a low rosette of narrow, wavy leaves heavily mottled and spotted in maroon-purple on both surfaces, from which short, dark-flushed spikes rise bearing small, starry, greenish-purple flowers with protruding, splayed tepals that give the plant its common name. Its miniature scale and boldly patterned foliage make it a striking specimen for containers, troughs, and the front of a warm, well-drained border where taller pineapple lilies would overwhelm it. Keep evenly moist through active summer growth, taper off as leaves yellow in fall, and store dry and frost-free over winter outside of the mildest zones.

common_name: Zambesi Pineapple Lily (Dwarf White Pineapple Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; more compact and slightly hardier than many larger pineapple lily species.

directions: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and mulch heavily over winter in zone 7-8 gardens or lift and store where winters are more severe. This compact southern African species forms a neat rosette of glossy, bright-green, strap-shaped leaves from which a dense, fragrant spike of small, pure white to greenish-white, star-shaped flowers rises in mid to late summer, topped with the characteristic tuft of leafy bracts. Its smaller stature and clean white bloom color make it a good choice for the front of a border or a large container where the bolder, taller Eucomis species would be out of scale, and its honey scent draws bees and other pollinators. Water regularly through summer growth and reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to prepare the bulb for winter dormancy.
